newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: Clinton hails progress in N.Korea nuclear project.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails progress in N.Korea nuclear project.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said Tuesday's ground-breaking for a nuclear project in North Korea was a "milestone" for peace on the Korean peninsula.

A U.S.-led international consortium broke ground in the northeastern town of Kumho for the project to build two 1,000-megawatt light-water reactors in return for Pyongyang's promise to freeze and eventually dismantle its suspected atomic weapons programme.

"We have now reached a major new milestone: ground breaking for the light-water reactor project," Clinton said in a statement read by U.S. Ambassador Paul Cleveland during the ground-breaking ceremony.
"Construction of the light-water reactors will contribute significantly to peace and stability of the Korean peninsula," the U.S. president said.

Clinton said Pyongyang's commitment to eventually accept nuclear safeguards and its use of light-water reactor technology, which makes it difficult to extract weapons-grade plutonium, were key to achieving global non-proliferation.

"This historic undertaking will require much hard work by each of the parties involved. But with a cooperative spirit, we can together help overcome decades of tension and hostility on the peninsula," he said.

The United States, along with South Korea and Japan, formed the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) in 1995, one year after it signed a landmark nuclear agreement with North Korea.
KEDO, responsible for financing the construction of the two reactors, has since been expanded to include Australia, Canada, Chile, Finland, Indonesia, New Zealand and the European Union.

The West had suspected that Pyongyang had secured enough plutonium to build one or two nuclear bombs and could try to sell them to a terrorist group to earn the hard currency needed to rescue the impoverished state from an economic crisis.

Under the 1994 U.S.-North Korean agreement signed in Geneva, North Korea pledged to allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to conduct special inspections of all its nuclear facilities to determine it had not hidden any weapons-grade plutonium that could be used to make a bomb.
Clinton said KEDO's success and implementing the 1994 nuclear agreement "are at the top of the United States' foreign policy agenda".
The two Koreas technically remain at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended without a peace treaty.
